title: Weight-based injections: mg/kg to mL to one or two decimal places
blurb: Turn a mg/kg or micrograms/kg prescription into a dose, then into the exact volume to draw up, rounded the way the stem asks.
question: A child weighing 18 kg is prescribed ondansetron 0.1 mg/kg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 4 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up?

teach.h: Two sums, in a fixed order
teach.body: Formal rule: dose = dose per kg × weight in kg; volume = (dose ÷ stock strength) × stock volume. Plain English: first find how much drug this person needs, then find how much liquid holds that much drug. Part A injection items usually include a weight-based dose, often for a child or a baby, and the answer is typed with its unit to one or two decimal places.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice papers (injection items); NMC ToC test specification

steps.label: Match units
steps.sub: micrograms or mg, same as the label

teach.caption: Keep every digit on the calculator until the very last step.

teach.h: Worked example: Leo on a children's ward
teach.body: Leo Hughes, 4, weighs 18 kg and is prescribed ondansetron 0.1 mg/kg IV. The ampoule says 4 mg in 2 mL. Dose: 0.1 × 18 = 1.8 mg. Volume: 1.8 ÷ 4 × 2 = 0.9 mL. Sense-check: 1.8 mg is a bit less than half of 4 mg, so the volume is a bit less than half of 2 mL. Type 0.9 mL.

Each wrong line is a real error pattern: label volume, inversion, skipped weight.

teach.text: The label "4 mg in 2 mL" is NOT 4 mg/mL. It is 2 mg in each mL. Forgetting to multiply by the 2 mL halves the volume. The same goes for "80 mg in 2 mL" or "100 mg in 2 mL": always finish with × stock volume.

teach.body: If the prescription is in micrograms/kg and the label is in mg, convert the dose to mg (÷ 1000) before you divide. 100 micrograms/kg × 15 kg = 1500 micrograms = 1.5 mg. Dividing 1500 by a label of 10 mg in 1 mL gives 150 mL, an impossible volume that tells you a conversion was missed.

items.label: typical answer range for IM or SC items

items: Dose = dose per kg × weight in kg (convert grams to kg first).
Volume = dose ÷ label strength × label volume.
Match micrograms and mg before dividing.
Classic errors: forgetting the 2 mL, inverting, skipping the weight step.
Round only the final answer, half-up, to the places the stem asks.

summary: You can now calculate a weight-based injection dose from mg/kg or micrograms/kg and turn it into the exact volume to draw up from any ampoule label. You can also round that volume correctly to one or two decimal places and spot an implausible answer.

A.q: A patient weighing 64 kg is prescribed pethidine 1 mg/kg by intramuscular injection. The ampoule label reads 50 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
A.why: Dose = 1 mg/kg × 64 kg = 64 mg. Volume = 64 ÷ 50 × 1 = 1.28 mL. Sense-check: 64 mg is a little more than one 50 mg ampoule, so a little more than 1 mL.

whyNot.0: This is have ÷ want (50 ÷ 64), the inverted fraction.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 2 as if the label were 50 mg in 2 mL; the label is 50 mg in 1 mL.
whyNot.3: This rounds to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

A.q: A child weighing 18 kg is prescribed ondansetron 0.1 mg/kg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 4 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: Dose = 0.1 × 18 = 1.8 mg. Volume = 1.8 ÷ 4 × 2 = 0.9 mL. Sense-check: 1.8 mg is just under half of 4 mg, so just under half of 2 mL.

whyNot.0: This forgets to multiply by the 2 mL stock volume (0.45 rounds to 0.5).
whyNot.1: This reads 0.1 mg/kg as 1 mg/kg, a tenfold error.
whyNot.2: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.

A.q: A child weighing 15 kg is prescribed morphine sulfate 100 micrograms/kg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.1: This converts 1500 micrograms to 15 mg (point moved one place too few).
whyNot.2: This converts 1500 micrograms to 0.15 mg (point moved one place too many).
whyNot.3: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.

B.q: A client weighing 58 kg is prescribed tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg by slow intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 500 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: Dose = 10 × 58 = 580 mg. Volume = 580 ÷ 500 × 5 = 5.8 mL. Sense-check: 580 mg is a bit more than one 500 mg ampoule, so a bit more than 5 mL.

whyNot.0: This forgets to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.1: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.
whyNot.3: This reads the strength as 50 mg/mL instead of 100 mg/mL (500 mg in 5 mL).

B.q: A man weighing 76 kg is prescribed gentamicin 5 mg/kg by intravenous infusion. The vial label reads 80 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: Dose = 5 × 76 = 380 mg. Volume = 380 ÷ 80 × 2 = 9.5 mL. Sense-check: 80 mg in 2 mL is 40 mg per mL, and 380 ÷ 40 = 9.5.

whyNot.1: This forgets to multiply by the 2 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.
whyNot.3: This doubles twice: it uses 40 mg per mL and then multiplies by 2 again.

B.q: A baby weighing 4.2 kg is prescribed gentamicin 5 mg/kg by intravenous injection. The vial label reads 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.
whyNot.1: This gives the dose in mg (21) as if it were the volume in mL.
whyNot.2: This reads 5 mg/kg as 0.5 mg/kg, a tenfold error.

C.q: A baby weighing 3650 g is prescribed ceftazidime 25 mg/kg by intravenous injection. The reconstituted vial contains 100 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
C.why: Weight: 3650 g = 3.65 kg. Dose = 25 × 3.65 = 91.25 mg. Volume = 91.25 ÷ 100 = 0.9125, which is 0.91 mL to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: This converts 3650 g to 36.5 kg (÷ 100 instead of ÷ 1000).
whyNot.3: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.

C.q: A child weighing 18.4 kg is prescribed ondansetron 150 micrograms/kg by intravenous infusion. The ampoule label reads 4 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: This forgets to multiply by the 2 mL stock volume.
whyNot.1: This converts micrograms to mg by ÷ 100, giving a tenfold error.
whyNot.3: This rounds to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

C.q: A man weighing 112 kg is prescribed pethidine 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 100 mg by intramuscular injection. The ampoule label reads 100 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: 1 mg/kg × 112 kg = 112 mg, which is above the 100 mg maximum, so the dose is 100 mg. Volume = 100 ÷ 100 × 2 = 2 mL.

whyNot.1: This gives 112 mg and misses the 100 mg maximum in the prescription.
whyNot.2: This misses the maximum and also forgets the 2 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: This caps the dose correctly but forgets the 2 mL stock volume.

reteach.title: Weight, dose, volume
reteach.question: A child weighing 20 kg is prescribed 0.5 mg/kg. The ampoule is 10 mg in 2 mL. What do you work out first?

blocks.body: First the dose: 0.5 × 20 = 10 mg. Then the volume: 10 ÷ 10 × 2 = 2 mL. Two short sums beat one long one, and you can sense-check each.

blocks.text: Writing the dose in mg straight into the answer box as if it were mL. 10 mg is not 10 mL: the label decides the volume.

explain.body: Multiply the dose per kg by the weight in kg. 2 mg/kg for a 75 kg person is 2 × 75 = 150 mg. This number is what you want.

test.q: A person weighing 75 kg is prescribed a medicine 2 mg/kg by intravenous injection. What dose should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: This divides the weight by the dose per kg instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: This drops a digit from the weight (7.5 kg), a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: This adds the numbers instead of multiplying them.

test.q: A child weighing 12 kg is prescribed a medicine 250 micrograms/kg. What is the dose in mg? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: This divides by 100, not 1000, a tenfold error.
whyNot.2: This divides by 10000, a tenfold error the other way.
whyNot.3: This gives the micrograms figure but labels it mg.

explain.body: Want ÷ have × stock volume. With 20 mg in 2 mL on the label, 45 mg needs 45 ÷ 20 × 2 = 4.5 mL.

test.q: A dose of 45 mg is needed. The ampoule label reads 20 mg in 2 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: This forgets the 2 mL stock volume (2.25 rounds to 2.3).
whyNot.1: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.
whyNot.2: This divides the dose by the stock volume instead of the strength.

test.q: A child weighing 9.7 kg is prescribed a medicine 0.15 mg/kg by intravenous injection. The ampoule label reads 2 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
test.why: Dose = 0.15 × 9.7 = 1.455 mg. Volume = 1.455 ÷ 2 = 0.7275, which is 0.73 mL to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: This cuts off the third decimal place instead of rounding 0.7275 up.
whyNot.2: This rounds to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.
whyNot.3: This is the inverted fraction: have ÷ want.
